interactions.summary: A parent wants to sit with Eve and understand her, Jiang replies that children are fully capable of this kind of manipulation, one student defends outsourcing care by analogy to food and water, Jiang questions whether credentialed strangers should outrank parents, and the room reframes the issue in terms of expertise versus parental risk and skin in the game.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang and multiple parents/students debating care, expertise, and responsibility

interactions.summary: Jiang escalates the therapist debate into a theological thought experiment about God delegating redemption to an infinitely wise alien species, and a student answers that the issue would depend on whether such beings preserved human freedom the way therapy ideally does.

speaker_notes.note: Several speakers in this packet are parents or speak from parental experience, which raises the practical pressure of the analogy beyond abstract theology.

claims.claim: A parent says the thought experiment matters to him because he has children and would first try to sit down with Eve and understand where she is coming from.
Jiang replies that this kind of destructive test is imaginable for real children and should not be dismissed as impossible simply because it is ugly.
A student argues that outsourcing help for a child should be no more scandalous than outsourcing food or water, because parents routinely rely on systems outside themselves.
Jiang counters that he does not understand why the class is so ready to believe a stranger with a PhD knows more about the child than the parent does.
The student answers that therapists know more about behavioral patterns than parents do, even if they do not know everything.
Another parent reframes the dispute as one of risk and skin in the game: the therapist may have tools, but the existential risk and final responsibility still fall on the parent.
Jiang tests the outsourcing logic theologically by asking whether God could have created an infinitely wise alien species to rule and reform humanity instead of sending the Son to crucify himself.
The student answers that such delegated help would be acceptable only if it won people over without coercion, preserving choice and free will in the way therapy ideally should.

chronology_notes.note: The packet evolves from practical parental debate about outsourcing care into Jiang's explicit theological analogy: if redemption could be delegated to competent outsiders, why did God choose self-sacrifice instead?

signature_moments.moment: The therapy defender normalizes outsourcing by comparing it to buying food and water rather than producing everything oneself for one's child.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the cleanest secular analogy for delegated care and therefore the strongest rival to Jiang's insistence on direct sacrificial involvement.

signature_moments.moment: The debate condenses into a sharp modern principle: expertise is not enough without skin in the game.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the therapist has different skin in the game
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That phrase translates the whole theological issue into risk, responsibility, and ownership, which makes it highly reusable later.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang pushes the therapy dispute into metaphysics by asking whether God could simply outsource salvation to an infinitely wise alien species.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The bizarre hypothetical is the packet's memorable hinge from modern psychology back to the necessity of incarnation.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A parent's term for the asymmetry between professional expertise and the existential responsibility borne by the parent.
The student's reason for thinking therapists know something parents do not: specialized knowledge of repeatable child behavior dynamics.
The student's ideal criterion for acceptable guidance: help should subtly orient someone toward the good without force, preserving their freedom of choice.
